author: Venkata Abhinandan Kancharla
text:
Most people are burning through Claude Fable for the wrong work.

They use the smartest model for everything:
• Brainstorming
• Small edits
• Formatting
• Rewriting sentences
• Fixing typos

That's like asking your senior engineer to spend the day renaming variables.

Fable is most valuable when the task requires judgment, strategy & deep reasoning.

A much better workflow is:

1. Plan with Fable
Use Fable to think through the problem, define the approach and outline what a great result should look like.

2. Execute with Sonnet or Haiku
Switch to a lighter model for the repetitive work writing the first draft, implementing the plan, making routine edits or handling straightforward coding tasks.

3. Review with Fable
Bring Fable back for the final critique. Let it identify gaps, challenge assumptions & improve the quality before you're done.

This simple workflow can dramatically reduce Fable usage while maintaining almost the same output quality.

A few other habits that help:
• Start a new chat for unrelated work instead of carrying massive context.
• Batch multiple requests into one prompt instead of sending dozens of messages.
• Keep frequently used documents in Projects instead of uploading them every session.
• Match the model to the complexity of the task instead of defaulting to Fable.

The takeaway is simple:
Don't use Fable to do everything.

Use it to think.
Let smaller models do the repetitive work.

Then let Fable make the final decisions.

"We've had the same senior ML role open since February."
A CTO told me that last week. Five months. Three offers out — two lost to bigger comp, one candidate who ghosted after the final round.

Transformer vs. RNN vs. CNN vs. GNN: Which AI Architecture Should You Learn?

Understanding the strengths of different neural network architectures is essential for anyone building a career in AI.

Transformer – Uses self-attention to process data in parallel, making it the foundation of modern LLMs and generative AI.

Applications: ChatGPT, translation, search, recommendation systems.
Valued by: OpenAI, Microsoft, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, NVIDIA, Meta.

RNN – Processes sequential data one step at a time, making it useful for time-series forecasting and signal processing.
Applications: Finance, predictive maintenance, speech recognition.
Valued by: JPMorgan Chase, Siemens, Honeywell, Philips.

CNN – Learns spatial patterns in images through convolutional filters.
Applications: Medical imaging, autonomous vehicles, manufacturing inspection.
Valued by: Tesla, Waymo, Apple, NVIDIA, Siemens Healthineers.

GNN – Learns from relationships in graph-structured data.
Applications: Fraud detection, recommendation engines, drug discovery, cybersecurity.
Valued by: Google, LinkedIn, Visa, Amazon, Palantir, Pfizer.

Each architecture solves a different class of problems. The best AI engineers understand not just how these models work, but when to use each one.

author: Maggie Yun
text:
OpenAI and Stripe are both hiring senior engineers right now. They're screening for completely different things first.

We analyzed 90 days of job descriptions from the companies hiring the most senior engineers.

We expected to find the one skill every company wanted.

We were wrong.

99% of job posting require AI/ML skills in AI companies OpenAI, Anthropic and Perplexity. Proficient in AI/ML is the price of the entry." 

However, 

At fintech and payments companies such as Stripe, JPMorganChase, AI/ML skill shows up in just 42% of job descriptions. What they screen for first is system design. They need people who build systems that don't fall over at 2am on payday.

Same skill is required at 99% level in one market; yet only 42% in another.
With same 8 years experience, you are facing completely different screening criteria.

That's why one company ghosts you while another moves you straight to interviews.

You're not applying to the market. You're applying to 3 or 4 different markets that each screen for something different first. Most engineers pitch the same version of themselves to companies that are looking for completely different strengths.

That's not a skill problem. It's a targeting problem. And no resume tweak fixes the wrong target.

Which market are you actually aiming at right now, AI, fintech, or infrastructure? 👇

I'm actively exploring opportunities as a Senior AI/ML Engineer, Generative AI Engineer, or Staff Machine Learning Engineer.

With 9+ years of experience, I've architected and deployed enterprise AI solutions across Banking, Healthcare, Insurance, and Capital Markets. My expertise spans Generative AI, LLMs, Agentic AI, GraphRAG, LangChain, LangGraph, Machine Learning, Python, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Kubernetes, AWS, Azure, GCP, and enterprise MLOps.

One production challenge that fundamentally changed how I evaluate AI systems was this:

Every model update looked better during testing, but we couldn't consistently prove it was better in production.
The prompts had improved.
The retrieval pipeline had been refined.
A newer model version was available.
Offline examples looked impressive.
The challenge wasn't building better AI.
It was measuring improvement objectively.

I worked on designing an evaluation framework that combined curated benchmark datasets, automated regression testing, LLM-as-a-judge evaluations, business-specific acceptance criteria, and human review for high-impact scenarios before every production release.

The objective wasn't simply:
"Did the model generate a good response?"
The better question was:
"Can we demonstrate, with measurable evidence, that this release is better than the previous one?"

That experience reinforced an important lesson:

Enterprise AI cannot rely on intuition alone. Every production release needs a repeatable evaluation strategy.

As AI platforms evolve, success depends on disciplined testing, measurable quality, and continuous validation not isolated demos or anecdotal results.
These are the engineering challenges I enjoy solving, and I'm excited to bring this experience to my next opportunity.

text:
High-resolution image and video experiments get harder when training, inference, and deployment live in separate tools.

SANA is an efficiency-oriented codebase for high-resolution image and video generation for researchers and ML engineers.

It helps you move from training to inference by providing complete pipelines, model configs, a model zoo, and deployment guidance around the SANA model family.

Key features:
• Image generation – text-to-image models and configs cover resolutions up to 4K.
• Video workflows – SANA-Video supports text-to-video and text-image-to-video generation.
• Efficient architecture – linear attention and 32× DC-AE compression reduce latent token counts.
• Adaptation tools – guidance covers LoRA, ControlNet, multi-scale training, and inference scaling.
• Deployment options – documented paths include Diffusers, ComfyUI, 4-bit/8-bit quantization, and SGLang.

It’s open-source (Apache 2.0 license).
